title: Add a Value to a Search Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary search tree (every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, every value in its right subtree is larger) and a value val that is not already in the tree.

Insert val as a new leaf: start at the root, go left when val is smaller and right when it is larger, and attach the new node at the first empty spot you reach. Do not rebalance or move any existing node. Return the root of the resulting tree.

Many valid search trees could hold the new value; this rule picks exactly one, so the output is unique.

examples.why: 5 < 6 goes left, 5 > 2 goes right, 5 > 4 goes right into an empty spot. The 5 becomes 4's right child.
An empty tree: the new node is the root.
12 sits between 10 and 15, so it becomes 15's left child, not a child of 5.

constraints: All values are distinct and val is not in the tree
The input is a valid binary search tree
hints: In a search tree, every comparison tells you which half the value belongs to. Where does a search for val end, given that val is not there?
The search walks down until it tries to step into a missing child. That empty spot is exactly where val belongs.
Walk from the root, going left or right by comparison, and keep the parent. When the next child is null, attach a new node there. Handle the empty tree separately.

explain.intuition:
Searching for a value that is not in the tree always ends by falling off the tree at some empty child pointer. Every comparison on the way agreed with the search tree rule, so putting the new node in that spot keeps the tree valid. No existing node moves.

The cost is the height of the tree: O(log n) when it is balanced, O(n) for a chain. This is the same walk as a lookup, which is why a plain search tree is a decent sorted index until the inserts arrive in sorted order and it degrades into a list.
steps: If root is null, return a new node with val.
If val < cur.val: if cur.left is null, attach the new node there and stop; otherwise move left. Mirror this for val > cur.val on the right.
pitfalls: Comparing only with the root and attaching to the root's child. In the third example 12 must go below 15, not below 5.
Returning the new node instead of the root.
Forgetting the empty tree: there is no parent to attach to, so the new node itself is the root.

solutions.title: Recursive descent
solutions.idea: Insert into the correct subtree and reattach what the recursive call returns. An empty subtree returns the new node.

solutions.title: Iterative walk
solutions.idea: Walk down by comparison until the next child is missing, then attach the new node there.

followups: Delete a value from the search tree instead. What do you do when the node has two children?
Inserting sorted values turns the tree into a chain. How do self-balancing trees such as AVL or red-black trees prevent that?
